Description of the practical

In this practical, we will use the RStudio Server available here: https://rstudio.dlab.elte.hu/. Please log in using the same username and password as you use with ssh login to the server.

After this lab, you will be able to:

  • To normalize the raw read counts using different methods
  • To explore and visualize count data
  • To do differential gene expression analysis
  • To visualize and understand the results

The Tasks and Questions will be denoted by boxes, as follows:

NoteT0 Q0

Questions to solve go here.

The dataset and the environment

The original count tables are from the recount2 database. It uses the SRA project code SRP029880. The experimental setup, along with additional accessory information, can be found on the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus under project code GSE50760.

Task 1: Setting up the environment

  • Create a directory named Transcriptomics_part_2 for the project.
  • Create a new RStudio server Project.
  • Open a new R Script file and save it.

Different normalization schemes

Comparison of the common normalization methods1
Normalization method Description Accounted factors Recommendations for use
CPM (counts per million) counts scaled by the total number of reads sequencing depth gene count comparisons between replicates of the same sample group; NOT for within-sample comparisons or DE analysis
TPM (transcripts per kilobase million) counts per length of transcript (kb) per million reads mapped sequencing depth and gene length gene count comparisons within a sample or between samples of the same sample group; NOT for DE analysis
RPKM/FPKM (reads/fragments per kilobase of exon per million reads/fragments mapped) similar to TPM sequencing depth and gene length gene count comparisons between genes within a sample; NOT for between-sample comparisons or DE analysis
DESeq2’s median of ratios counts divided by sample-specific size factors determined by the median ratio of gene counts relative to the geometric mean per gene sequencing depth and RNA composition gene count comparisons between samples and for DE analysis; NOT for within-sample comparisons
edgeR’s trimmed mean of M values (TMM) uses a weighted trimmed mean of the log expression ratios between samples sequencing depth and RNA composition gene count comparisons between and within samples, and for DE analysis

Computing different normalization schemes in R

Important

We try out multiple normalization methods to get familiar with them and assess their impact on the counts. During a normal analysis, we apply only a single normalization method!

Here, we will use a subset of the RNA-seq count table from a colorectal cancer study. We have filtered the original count table to include only protein-coding genes (to improve calculation speed) and selected five metastasized colorectal cancer samples and five normal colon samples. There is an additional column width that contains the length of the corresponding gene in base pairs. The length of the genes is important to compute RPKM and TPM values.

CPM (Counts Per Million) normalization

CPM of a single gene from a single sample:

\(CPM = \frac{\text{Nr. of read counts of the gene × } 10^{6}}{\text{Total nr. of counted reads}}\)

CPM of all genes of all samples (excluding the width column):

cpm <- apply(X = counts[, 1:10], 
             MARGIN = 2, 
             FUN = function(x) x/sum(as.numeric(x)) * 10^6)

RPKM (Reads Per Kilo base of transcript per Million mapped reads) normalization

RPKM of a single gene from a single sample:

\(RPKM = \frac{\text{Nr. of read counts of the gene × } 10^{3} × 10^{6}}{\text{Total nr. of counted reads × Gene length}}\)

RPKM of all genes of all samples:

# create a vector of gene lengths 
geneLengths <- counts$width

# compute rpkm 
rpkm <- apply(X = counts[, 1:10], 
              MARGIN = 2, 
              FUN = function(x) 10^9 * x / geneLengths / sum(as.numeric(x)))

Task 4: Exploring the RPKM values

NoteT4 Q1

Summarize the distribution of \(log_{2}\) RPKM-normalized counts using boxplots.

NoteT4 Q2

Which samples have the lowest and the highest RPKM values on average? (Include the code in your answer as well.)

The above-mentioned normalization methods are also explained in this StatQuest video.

None of the CPM, RPKM/FPKM (and TPM) metrics account for another important confounding factor when comparing expression levels of genes across samples: library composition, which may also be referred to as the relative size of the compared transcriptomes. This factor is not dependent on the sequencing technology; it is rather biological. For instance, when comparing transcriptomes across different tissues, some genes in one tissue can consume a large fraction of reads, whereas in the other tissue, they are not expressed at all. This kind of imbalance in the composition of compared transcriptomes can lead to wrong conclusions about which genes are actually differentially expressed. This consideration is addressed in two popular R packages: DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2010), each with a different algorithm. edgeR uses a normalization procedure called Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM). DESeq2 implements a normalization procedure using Median of Ratios, which is obtained by finding the ratio of the log-transformed count of a gene divided by the average of the log-transformed values of the gene in all samples (geometric mean), and then taking the median of these values for all genes. The raw read count for each gene is finally divided by this value (the median of the ratios) to obtain normalized counts. In order to see a demonstration of DESeq2’s normalization method, see the Differential expression analysis section.

The normalization method of DESeq2 is explained in this StatQuest video.

Exploratory analysis of the read count table

A typical quality control, in this case, interrogating the RNA-seq experiment design, is to measure the similarity among samples in terms of the quantified expression level profiles across a set of genes. One important observation to make is whether the most similar samples to any given sample are its biological replicates. This can be computed using unsupervised clustering techniques such as hierarchical clustering and visualized as a heatmap with dendrograms. Another commonly applied technique is Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which is visualized as a two-dimensional (or, in some cases, three-dimensional) scatter plot. PCA is a technique used to emphasize variation and bring out strong patterns in a dataset. It’s often used to make data easy to explore and visualize. See some detailed visual explanations here.

Clustering the samples and the genes based on their expression levels

WWe can combine clustering and heatmap visualization of the results using the heatmap functions available in various R libraries. The basic R installation comes with the stats::heatmap function. However, there are other libraries available in CRAN (e.g., pheatmap (Kolde 2019) and the geom_tile function of ggplot2) or Bioconductor (e.g., ComplexHeatmap (Gu, Eils, and Schlesner 2016)) that offer greater flexibility and more appealing visualizations.

The drawing and the interpretation of heatmaps are explained in this StatQuest video.

Here, we demonstrate a heatmap using the pheatmap package and the previously calculated RPKM normalized read counts. As these matrices can be quite large, both computing the clustering and rendering the heatmaps can consume substantial resources and time. Therefore, a quick and informative way to compare samples is to select a subset of genes that are, for instance, most variable across samples, and use that subset to do the clustering and visualization.

Let’s select the top 100 most variable genes among the samples:

# compute the variance of each gene across samples
V <- apply(rpkm, 1, var)

# sort the results by variance in decreasing order and select the top 100 genes 
selectedGenes <- names(V[order(V, decreasing = T)][1:100])

Now we can quickly produce a heatmap where samples and genes are clustered:

library(pheatmap)

pheatmap(rpkm[selectedGenes, ], scale = 'row', show_rownames = FALSE)

PCA (Principal Component Analysis) of the samples based on the RPKM normalized counts of the top 100 most variable genes

If you need an explanation about the PCA method, please watch this StatQuest video.

Let’s make a PCA plot to see the clustering of replicates as a scatter plot in two dimensions.

library(stats)
library(ggplot2)
# ggfortify package is needed to let ggplot2 know about PCA data structure. 
library(ggfortify) 

# transpose the matrix 
M <- t(rpkm[selectedGenes, ])

# transform the counts to log2 scale 
M <- log2(M + 1)

# compute PCA 
pcaResults <- prcomp(M)

# plot PCA results making use of ggplot2's autoplot function
autoplot(pcaResults, 
         data = colData, 
         colour = 'group')

We should observe whether the samples from the case group (CASE) and the control group (CTRL) can be split into two distinct clusters on the scatter plot of the first two largest principal components (PC1 and PC2).

Differential expression analysis

Differential expression analysis allows us to test tens of thousands of hypotheses (one test per gene) against the null hypothesis that the gene’s activity remains the same across two conditions. There are multiple limiting factors that influence the power to detect genes with real changes between two biological conditions. Among these are the limited number of biological replicates, non-normality in the distribution of read counts, and greater measurement uncertainty for lowly expressed genes than for highly expressed genes (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014). Tools such as edgeR and DESeq2 address these limitations by using sophisticated statistical models to maximize the amount of knowledge that can be extracted from noisy datasets.

An external video about differential expression analysis is available here.

DESeq2

  1. Normalizes the read counts by computing size factors, which addresses the differences not only in the library sizes, but also in the library compositions.
  2. FFor each gene, it estimates the dispersion of the gene across biological replicates. The dispersion value computed by DESeq2 is equal to the squared coefficient of variation (variation divided by the mean).
  3. A line is fitted across the dispersion estimates of all genes computed in 2) versus the mean normalized counts of the genes.
  4. Dispersion values of each gene are shrunken towards the fitted line in 3).
  5. A Generalized Linear Model (GLM) is fitted, accounting for additional confounding variables related to the experimental design, such as sequencing batches, treatment, temperature, patient age, sequencing technology, etc.
  6. For a given contrast (e.g., treatment type: drug-A versus untreated), a test for differential expression is carried out against the null hypothesis that the log fold change of the normalized counts of the gene in the given pair of groups is exactly zero.
  7. Adjusts p-values for multiple testing.

In order to carry out a differential expression analysis using DESeq2, three kinds of inputs are necessary:

  1. The read count table must contain raw read counts as integers, not processed by any normalization technique. The rows represent features (e.g., genes, transcripts, genomic intervals) and columns represent samples.
  2. A colData table: this table describes the experimental design.
  3. A design formula: this formula describes the variable of interest in the analysis (e.g., treatment status) along with (optionally) other covariates (e.g., batch, temperature, sequencing technology).

Let’s define these inputs:

# remove the 'width' column and convert the data.frame to a matrix
countData <- as.matrix(counts[, 1:10])

# define the experimental setup: 
# we already have the colData variable

# define the design formula based on the "group" column of colData
designFormula <- "~ group"

We are now ready to run DESeq2.

library(DESeq2)

# create a DESeq dataset object from the count matrix and the colData 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = countData, 
                              colData = colData, 
                              design = as.formula(designFormula))

# print dds object to see the contents
print(dds)
class: DESeqDataSet 
dim: 19719 10 
metadata(1): version
assays(1): counts
rownames(19719): TSPAN6 TNMD ... MYOCOS HSFX3
rowData names(0):
colnames(10): CASE_1 CASE_2 ... CTRL_4 CTRL_5
colData names(2): source_name group

The DESeqDataSet object contains all the information about the experimental setup, the read counts, and the design formulas. Certain functions can be used to access this information separately: rownames(dds) shows which features are used in the study (e.g., genes), colnames(dds) displays the studied samples, counts(dds) displays the count table, and colData(dds) displays the experimental setup.

Remove genes that have almost no information in any of the given samples.

# For each gene, we count the total number of reads for that gene in all samples 
# and remove those that don't have at least 1 read. 
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds)) > 1, ]

Now, we can use the DESeq function from the DESeq2 package, which is a wrapper that implements estimation of size factors to normalize the counts, estimation of dispersion values, and fitting a GLM model based on the experimental design formula. This function returns a DESeqDataSet object, an updated version of the dds variable we pass to the function as input.

dds <- DESeq(dds)

Diagnostic plots

At this point, before proceeding with any downstream analysis and jumping to conclusions about the biological insights that are achievable with the experimental data at hand, it is important to run additional diagnostic tests to improve our confidence in the data quality and experimental setup.

PCA plot

A final diagnosis is to check the biological reproducibility of the sample replicates in a PCA plot or a heatmap. Normalized counts can be transformed using the DESeq2::rlog function, and the DESeq2::plotPCA can be readily used to plot the PCA results.

rld <- rlog(dds)

plotPCA(rld,
        ntop = 500,
        intgroup = 'group')

Task 7: Understanding the PCA plot

NoteT7 Q1

Why is this PCA plot a bit different from the previous PCA plot?

The RLE (Relative Log Expression) plot

The RLE plot is useful for determining whether the data at hand require normalization (Gandolfo and Speed 2018). Sometimes, even the datasets normalized using the explained methods above may need further normalization due to unforeseen sources of variation that might stem from the library preparation, the person who carries out the experiment, the date of sequencing, the temperature changes in the laboratory at the time of library preparation, and so on and so forth. An RLE plot is a quick diagnostic that can be applied to raw or normalized count matrices to determine whether further processing is required.

Let’s generate RLE plots of raw counts and normalized counts using the EDASeq package (Risso et al. 2011).

library(EDASeq)

# plot the 2 plots next to each other
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# plot 1 is using the raw read counts
plotRLE(countData, 
        outline = FALSE, 
        ylim = c(-4, 4), 
        col = c(rep("darkred", 5), rep("gray", 5)),
        main = 'Raw Counts', 
        las = 2)

# plot 2 is using the normalized counts
plotRLE(counts(dds, normalized = TRUE),
        outline = FALSE, 
        ylim = c(-4, 4),
        col = c(rep("darkred", 5), rep("gray", 5)),
        main = 'Normalized Counts', 
        las = 2)

Here, the RLE plot comprises boxplots, where each boxplot represents the distribution of the relative log expression of the genes expressed in the corresponding sample. Each gene’s expression is divided by the median expression value of that gene across all samples. Then this is transformed to a log scale, which gives the relative log expression value for a single gene. The RLE values for all the genes from a sample are visualized as a boxplot.

Ideally, the boxplots are centered around the horizontal zero line and are as tightly distributed as possible (Risso et al. 2014). From the plots we made for the raw and normalized count data, we can observe that the normalized dataset has improved upon the raw count data across all samples. However, in some cases, it is important to visualize RLE plots in combination with other diagnostic plots such as PCA plots, heatmaps, and correlation plots to see if there is more unwanted variation in the data, which can be further accounted for using packages such as RUVseq (Risso et al. 2014) and sva (Leek et al. 2012).

Differentially expressed genes

Now, we can compare and contrast the samples based on different variables of interest. In this case, we currently have only one variable: the group variable that determines whether a sample belongs to the CASE group or the CTRL group.

# compute the contrast for the 'group' variable where 'CTRL' samples are used as the control group. 
DEresults <- results(dds, 
                     contrast = c("group", 'CASE', 'CTRL'))

# sort results by increasing p-value
DEresults <- DEresults[order(DEresults$pvalue), ]

Thus, we have obtained a table of the differential expression status of case samples relative to control samples.

It is important to note that the sequence of the elements in the contrast argument determines which group of samples is used as the control. This impacts how the results are interpreted; for instance, if a gene is found up-regulated (has a positive \(log_{2}\) fold change), its up-regulation status is only relative to the factor provided as the control. In this case, we used samples from the CTRL group as controls and contrasted the samples from the CASE group with them. Thus, genes with a positive \(log_{2}\) fold change are called up-regulated in the case samples with respect to the control, while genes with a negative \(log_{2}\) fold change are down-regulated in the case samples. Whether the deregulation is significant or not warrants an assessment of the adjusted p-values.

Let’s have a look at the contents of the DEresults table.

# shows a summary of the results
print(DEresults)

The first three lines of this output show the contrast and the statistical test used to compute these results, along with the dimensions of the resulting table (number of columns and rows). Below these lines is the actual table with 6 columns:

  • baseMean represents the average normalized expression of the gene across all considered samples.
  • log2FoldChange represents the base-2 logarithm of the fold change of the normalized expression of the gene in the given contrast.
  • lfcSE represents the standard error of the \(log_{2}\) fold change estimate, and
  • stat is the statistic calculated in the contrast,
  • which is translated into a pvalue and
  • adjusted for multiple testing in the padj column.

You can read about the correction of p-values for multiple testing here and/or watch a Statquest video.

Visualization of DE results

MA plot

The MA plot is a scatter plot that shows the \(log_{2}\) fold change of the genes on the y-axis and mean normalized counts on the x-axis. The MA plot is a useful diagnostic tool to visualize the distribution of the p-values and the \(log_{2}\) fold changes. The genes that are significantly differentially expressed are usually located at the top or bottom of the plot, while the genes that are not significantly differentially expressed are located in the middle.

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
plotMA(object = dds, ylim = c(-5, 5))

Volcano plot

The volcano plot is a scatter plot that shows the \(log_{2}\) fold change of the genes on the x-axis and the \(-log_{10}\) p-value on the \(y\)-axis. The volcano plot is a useful diagnostic tool to visualize the distribution of the p-values and the \(log_{2}\) fold changes. The genes that are significantly differentially expressed are usually located at the top or bottom of the plot, while the genes that are not significantly differentially expressed are located in the middle.

library(EnhancedVolcano)

 EnhancedVolcano(DEresults,
    lab = rownames(DEresults),
    x = 'log2FoldChange',
    y = 'pvalue')
